scout.purpose: Treating behaviour as a value lets Kotlin APIs separate a reusable operation from the policy supplied by each caller.
scout.realWorldUse: Compose event callbacks, collection operators, coroutine builders, configuration blocks, listeners, and test helpers all rely on lambdas and function types.
scout.outcome: Read function types, write focused lambdas and higher-order functions, and use extensions or scope functions without hiding control flow.

blocks.text: A function type describes inputs and output, such as (Expense) -> Boolean for a rule that receives an Expense and returns a Boolean. A lambda is an unnamed function value. Its parameters appear before -> and its last expression becomes the result. Higher-order functions accept or return functions. This is how filter receives a caller-defined predicate while keeping traversal reusable. Give complex lambdas named functions when the policy deserves a domain name or is reused.

blocks.code:
val isLarge: (Expense) -> Boolean = { expense ->
    expense.amount >= 100.0
}

fun countMatching(
    expenses: List<Expense>,
    predicate: (Expense) -> Boolean,
): Int = expenses.count(predicate)
blocks.caption: The higher-order function owns iteration and the supplied lambda owns the matching policy.

blocks.text: An extension function is called with receiver syntax but does not modify the receiver class or gain private access. Resolution is static from the declared receiver type, so an extension cannot provide runtime polymorphism. Extensions work well for focused transformations closely associated with an existing type, especially at application boundaries. Avoid broad public extensions with generic names because they pollute completion and can collide. Keep visibility as narrow as practical.

blocks.code:
fun String.toPositiveAmountOrNull(): Double? =
    trim().toDoubleOrNull()?.takeIf { it > 0.0 }

fun Expense.formatted(): String =
    "${category.displayName()}: £%.2f".format(amount)
blocks.caption: Each extension adds a small domain operation while using only the receiver public API.

blocks.title: No new member exists
blocks.text: Extension dispatch is static. If subtype-specific behaviour is required, use a member or interface contract instead.

sections.title: Use scope functions for one clear purpose

blocks.text: let, run, with, apply, and also execute a block with an object in scope, but differ in receiver name and returned value. Choose from intent: apply configures and returns the receiver; also performs an additional side effect and returns the receiver; let transforms using it; run computes using this; with is a non-extension form. Deep nesting and switching between this and it make control flow opaque. A normal local variable is often clearer.

blocks.code:
val draft = ExpenseDraft().copy(category = "Food")

val amount = rawAmount
    .toPositiveAmountOrNull()
    ?.also { println("Parsed amount: $it") }
    ?: return
blocks.caption: The extension owns parsing, also observes the present value, and Elvis exits on absence.

trap_check.mistake: Nesting several scope functions using both this and it.
trap_check.why: The reader loses track of receivers, returned values, and early exits.
trap_check.fix: Name intermediate values or replace the nesting with ordinary statements.

trap_check.mistake: Expecting an extension to override a member at runtime.
trap_check.why: Extensions are resolved statically and members take precedence.
trap_check.fix: Use an interface or open member for polymorphic behaviour.

challenge_intro.task: Add parsing and formatting extensions plus a higher-order report function that accepts different expense-selection policies.
challenge_intro.successLooksLike: Function types make selection policy explicit. Extensions remain focused and have narrow visibility. The solution avoids nested scope-function chains.
